content: The document is a detailed exploration of school health services (SHS) globally, conducted in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO). It provides a comprehensive review of SHS frameworks, methodologies, and findings, with a focus on their structure, coordination, and implementation at national and subnational levels. 1. Collaboration with WHO Guidelines: This document is part of the WHO guideline on school health services and is publicly available for transparency and informational purposes. It adheres to the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014). 2. Licensing and Usage: The publication is licensed under Creative Commons, allowing non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and adaptations must follow the same or equivalent licensing terms. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation. 3. The responsibility for the interpretation and use of the material lies with the reader, and WHO is not liable for any damages arising from its use. 4. Methodology of the Exploratory Review: The review was conducted to examine SHS frameworks or models globally, focusing on their structure, coordination, and integration within health systems. The review was pragmatic, not representative, and aimed to include examples from each WHO region and income level. 5. Search Strategy: A three-week online search in December 2019 used PubMed, Google, and other sources to identify SHS frameworks. The search prioritized recent literature (2015–2019) but included older materials for context. Search terms included combinations of school health, health system, framework, policy, and country or region names. 6. Case Studies: The review included case studies from eight countries, representing all six WHO regions and four income levels (low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income, and high-income countries). These case studies highlighted the main characteristics of SHS frameworks, including their lead sectors and organizational structures. 7. Findings on SHS Frameworks: Published reviews often focused on whole-school health programs, such as the Health-Promoting Schools (HPS) Framework and the FRESH initiative, but sometimes marginalized the SHS component. Local-level SHS frameworks examined whether services were delivered at schools or in the community, their structure, and whether dedicated personnel were involved. 8. Examples of SHS Frameworks: Rwanda: The Ministry of Education's national school health policy assigns responsibility for SHS to the Ministry of Health, with nurses visiting schools quarterly. However, this is not consistently implemented. The policy includes a minimum package of services, such as gender-based violence referral and first-aid kits. Bangladesh: School health clinics are staffed by medical officers, pharmacists, and support staff. Services include intermittent screening and referrals. Health education officers train teachers to provide first aid and health education. Lao People's Democratic Republic: The Ministry of Education and Sport leads SHS implementation, with limited coverage achieved through NGO collaboration. Services include iron supplementation and deworming, coordinated by school health focal-point teachers. Egypt: School children are required to have school health insurance. The SHS framework includes disease prevention and health-care services, with a focus on health education and screening. 9. Acknowledgments and Contributors: The guideline development involved experts from various fields, including child and adolescent health, public health, and education. Financial support was provided by the UK Department for International Development, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and the US Agency for International Development. 10. Purpose of the Review: The exploratory review aimed to provide insights into SHS frameworks globally, focusing on their organization, delivery, and integration within broader health systems. It serves as a resource for policymakers and stakeholders to improve SHS implementation and outcomes.
